entry.content:
Everything felt off.
He knew that before anything else.
Though he wasn't even conscious yet—he just…

Knew.

Sound crept in, surfacing from the darkness.
Faint impressions of swaying, rustling, a world breathing.
Around him were voices, echoing along the distant edge of perception.

Thought came next—unfocused—reaching.

This isn't my home.
Where am I?

The outside voices rattled on, falling flat against the surface of his mind.
He tightened his concentration, focusing in on the words.

There was a young voice, hushed and urgent.

“You think he's civil?”

A steadier one—feminine.

“He's wild.”

Another—low and rough.

“And what do you plan on doing with him?”
“If he dies, he dies. Nothing we can do about it.”

Concern ran through their voices, but thin—like tending a sick dog.

He shifted on what he expected to be a firm spring mattress under soft covers.
Instead, the surface beneath him was coarse and gritty, and his cover was rough and weathered.

This isn't my cover or my bed.
What's going on?
Am I dreaming?

He inhaled— And the smells hit all at once. Damp earth, rotting leaves, and something warm—close, living. They were wild, unfamiliar, and all of them too strong.

His breath caught as his mind tried—and failed—to make sense of it.

“He's stirring,” said the rough voice.

Then the steady one:

“Chatter, come'ere.”
“If he bolts, let him.”

He raised a hand to rub his eyes, but when it got close—

Bonk.

“Nyeh,” he moaned.

His hand hit his face too soon.
He moved his hand again with more care and he felt it—something long and thin.
It was his face, but it was shaped wrong.

Then he opened his eyes to find his hand… wasn't a hand.
He held it out in front of him.

Claws.
Beans.
Fur.

A paw.

He stared at it, waiting for the image to correct itself.

It didn't

The young one swallowed audibly.

“…Snout.”

The rough voice answered next, low and puzzled, as if trying to make sense of the strange behavior.

“He don’t recognize himself.”

He tore his gaze from his would-be hand and looked at the ones talking.

Old-style clothes.
Simple.
Browns, tans, and greys.

Then he realized what they were.

A coyote crouched low in concern.
An otter leaned in with eyes like golf-balls.
A bobcat stood upright behind them, arms crossed—analyzing.

He couldn't help but feel how small he was surrounded by them.

The coyote extended a paw toward him, a gentle signal to stay still.

“Easy now.”
“Can ya' understand me?”

He blinked and tilted his head.

“Uh… Yeah?…” he mumbled.

The coyote lowered her paw, nodding.

“I'm Snout.”
“And you?”

“I- I'm Joseph.”
“What's going on?”
“Where am I?”

The otter's whiskers twitched.

“That ain't a local name.”

“No, it ain't,” replied the bobcat.

“You're in the Spine Weaver forest.”
“A day's walk to Flint Water,” Snout finished.

Joseph stared with blinking wide eyes—mouth slightly agape.

“…Huh?”

They all went quiet.

The otter stepped forward.

“You don't know Flint Water?”

“Every fox within three rivers knows Flint,” said the bobcat.

Fox?

The word snagged.

Is that what I am?

Snout chimed in, voice low.

“What do you remember?” “Anything before this?”

“Like, where's your clothes?” the otter chimed in.

Joseph blinked, then examined himself.
The cover had slid below his shoulders, and he was wearing nothing but fur.

“I-I-”

He stammered, pulling the cover to his neck—discretely.

“I don't know.”
“The last thing I remember, I was home in bed.”

Joseph swallowed.

“I don't remember anything strange happening before waking up here.”

Everyone went silent again.
The coyote and bobcat exchanged glances, and the otter looked between them.

“Could be lyin',” said the bobcat.

Snout’s gaze sharpened immediately.

The bobcat huffed and raised his paws.

“Whatever, I don't know how to handle this.”
“I'm getting Eli.”

He walked into the brush—his absence leaving the lingering sound of whispering trees.
A pressing silence.

Snout exhaled slowly through her nose, her posture easing just a fraction.
Her gaze shifted, flicking briefly to the otter.

Chatter leaned in closer to her, lowering his voice without meaning to.

“I mean—if he’s not lyin’, then what does that even—”

“We'll figure that out,” Snout said, steady.

Not looking at Joseph now—thinking.

Joseph was becoming increasingly aware of himself.

Low to the ground, folded in on himself, surrounded by bodies that stood upright where he should have been standing.

But he wasn’t.

He felt small— Vulnerable.

Something in his chest tightened.

He pulled the rough cover tighter around himself, clutching it with both paws.
The motion felt clumsy, imprecise—like trying to tie knots with numb fingers.

He leaned forward, propped himself against his arms, and pushed up.

His limbs didn’t line up right.
His weight tipped too far forward, then too far back.
His shoulders hunched instinctively, spine curling where it shouldn’t.

Still—he pushed.
His legs straightened.
For a moment—just a moment—he rose.
Too tall, unsteady, wrong.

He looked ahead where the otter’s voice carried on, half-whispered:

“I mean, you think he’s telling the truth, or—”

He tilted.

Thud.

Joseph hit the ground—breath knocked out of him.

The cover wrapped his limbs.
One of his legs kicked uselessly against it, not bending the way he expected—joint catching at an angle that made no sense in his mind.

The otter and coyote turned their heads.

“…what was that?” said the otter.

Joseph sucked in air, sharp and uneven.

No. Get up. Come on—get up.

He shifted till the cover no longer restricted him and rose.
This time faster, more desperate.
He pushed against his arms again, forcing his body upward—but everything resisted.
His balance pitched forward immediately, his weight sitting in the wrong places, his center pulled somewhere beneath his chest instead of above his hips.

His back twisted, and his legs locked.
For a fraction of a second, he made it higher than before—

Then everything slipped.

He collapsed again—harder this time, shoulder striking first, then the side of his face against the grit.

The world jolted.

Joseph lay there, stunned—air dragging back into his lungs in shallow, uneven pulls.

Then he planted his paws again.
Tried to push himself up—

“Stop.”

Snout’s voice cut through—firm—right beside him now.

“You’re going to hurt yourself.”

Joseph froze, halfway lifted.
His body wavered—uncertain whether to obey her or the instinct clawing at him to fix this.

“What’s wrong?” she asked, steady—non-accusing.
“What’s not working?”

Joseph swallowed, breath hitching.

“I—”

The words didn’t come.
He glanced down at himself—at the limbs that bent wrong, the weight that sat wrong, the balance that refused to exist.

How do you explain inheriting the shape of a different body?

“I can’t—”

He stopped.
Shook his head.
It wasn’t that he couldn’t stand, not exactly.
It was—

This is wrong.

“I don’t know,” he said instead, voice thin.

Chatter shifted closer, eyes darting over him.

“You mean you’re hurt, or—like—you can’t feel your legs, or—”

“I can feel them,” Joseph said, quick.
“That’s not—” he cut himself off, shaking his head.

He tried again to adjust his footing—just to sit higher—but his arms bent weird and he slipped, forcing him back down.
Frustration flared sharp in his chest.

Why can’t I—

The brush rustled.
All three of them turned.

The bobcat pushed through first—but Joseph barely registered him.
The one behind him drew his attention just by his presence.

A red wolf stepped into the clearing.
Muted reds along his coat, darkened where the light didn’t catch.
Pale scars crossed his face—old, clean lines that didn’t fade into the fur.
He carried himself differently from the others—no hesitation, no adjustment to the space.

Joseph felt the difference immediately.
Not just taller, but solid in a way the others weren’t.

Joseph’s chest tightened.
He felt small before, but now?…

The wolf’s gaze passed over the group once—quick, efficient—then settled on Joseph.

“That him?” he asked.

“That’s him,” the bobcat—said.
“Doesn’t know where he is. Says he just woke.”

The wolf stepped closer.
Measured, unhurried.

“You remember anything?” he asked.

Joseph hesitated.

“I- No- I don't.”

“Scruff said you were convulsing when they found you,” the wolf said.
“Crying out.”

Joseph blinked.

“…I— I don’t remember that.”

“Mm.”

The wolf lowered—not enough to match Joseph, not even close, but just enough to close the distance.

“No clothes. No memory. You don’t know where you are.”
“That about right?”

Joseph nodded faintly.

The wolf studied him a moment longer.

“Something’s wrong,” he stated.

Joseph stiffened.

“I’m fine,” he said, too quickly.

Snout’s gaze snapped back to him.

“No, you’re not.”

The bobcat huffed.

“His head ain't right.”

Snout’s ears flicked back.

“Don’t start, Scruff.”

“I’m sayin’ what it is.”

“You don’t know that.”

“Look at him.”

“I see him.”

Their voices didn’t rise—but the edge was there.

Joseph felt it building around him.

“Fox was shaking in the dirt,” Scruff went on.
“Now he says he’s fine?”

“He’s disoriented,” Snout said.
“That’s not the same thing.”

“Or he’s lost it.”

That landed.
Something in Joseph twisted.

“That’s enough,” Eli snapped at the two.

Then, to Joseph:

“You don’t want to say it.”

Joseph’s ears flicked.

“…You wouldn’t get it,” he muttered.

The words hung there alone for a moment, then Eli spoke again:

“Try me.”

Joseph shook his head.
Harder this time.

“I- I just—”

He looked down again.
At his paws.
At the ground.
At anything but them.

“It’s wrong,” he said.

His voice thin, barely there.
The silence stretched—tightened.

Then—

“It’s not right,” he forced out. “Everything’s wrong—this—”

He motioned at himself, sudden, frantic.

“I’m not—this—”

He shook his head sharply.

“I’m not a fox!”

He dragged in another breath.

“I’m— I’m human.”

Silence.

Chatter blinked.

“…A what?”

Snout frowned, trying to follow.

“You’re… saying you’re not a fox…”

Careful, grounding.

Scruff didn’t hesitate.

“His head really ain't right.”

“Stop,” Snout snapped, sharper now.

“What, you believe that?”

“I didn’t say that.”

“Then what are you sayin’?”

“Don’t push him right now.”

Joseph’s chest tightened.

Their voices blurred.
They remained tempered, but pressed in regardless.
On him—around him—through him.

He didn’t have anything left to give them.
The words—the explanations—none of it mattered.

He dropped back down, folding in on himself—paws pressing hard against his eyes.
Just… done.

The wolf straightened and silence settled again, different now.

“Snout, Scruff, Chatter.”

They looked up immediately.

“Find him something to wear.”

Snout held his gaze for a moment, then nodded once.

“…Alright.”

Chatter glanced once more at Joseph—hesitating—but followed.

Scruff lingered half a second longer.
Then turned without a word.

The three of them moved off through the brush—quiet.
They understood.

The clearing stilled.

Joseph didn’t move.

The wolf stepped closer, and paused.
Then extended a hand—a paw.

“Hey.”

No response.

“You’re not staying down there.”
“Do you want help, or not?”

Slowly, he lowered his paws from his eyes.
He looked at the paw, then up at him.
That same steady, unreadable expression.

Waiting.

Joseph swallowed.

“…Yeah.”

Quiet, reluctant.

He shifted, clutching the rough cover tight around himself with one paw as he reached out with the other.
Their hands met in a firm grasp.

Joseph pulled.
His legs wobbled immediately, balance pitching—but the wolf adjusted, guiding him.

Joseph held the cover tighter around himself as he rose to his feet.
His legs quivered, but he stood—he was upright.
He froze there, breath tight.
Waiting for the fall—

But Eli's hand held him in place.

“Easy,” the wolf said.

After a moment, the grip eased—just slightly.

Joseph swayed, focused—finding where his weight actually was.

The others returned, brush shifting as they stepped back into the clearing—bundles of cloth in their arms.
They slowed when they saw him standing.

Snout’s eyes flicked from Joseph to the wolf—taking it in.

“…He’s up.”

The wolf didn’t look away from Joseph and simply nodded.

“He’s staying with us.”
“We'll camp here till he's ready to move.”

Scruff’s ears snapped forward.

“You’re serious?”

“He’s not walking out of here like that,” the wolf said.

Scruff frowned.

“We don’t know what he is.”

“We know enough,” the wolf replied.
“He was alone. No supplies. No memory.”
“You want to leave him out here like this?”

Scruff’s jaw shifted.
No answer.

Snout stepped in before it could turn.

“We’ll make it work,” she said.

Chatter nodded quickly.

“Yeah—yeah, we can—we can do it—”

Joseph didn’t hear most of it.
His focus had narrowed again—down to the ground beneath him.
To the way his weight shifted.
To how wrong it still felt.

But—

Carefully, he shifted one paw forward.
It landed uneven.
His weight followed late and his body lurched—
He caught himself.
Adjusted.

Another step.
Clumsy—unsteady.

He was walking—
that was real—
even if nothing else made sense.

entry.content:
Joseph’s eyes opened to tent canvas.
His snout was cold from the night air.

His first thoughts rose clear and sharp.

I’m done.

It arrived whole, like it had been waiting on the other side of sleep.

The canvas above him held the faint gray of early morning. Wind dragged cold along the seams. Somewhere outside, a bird called once and went quiet again.

Joseph stared.

His chest already hurt.

Not the sharp hurt of being struck, or scraped, or hungry.

A slow, constant weight—like he’d gone to bed with a stone pressed against his heart and woken to find it had grown roots.

He lay still, blanket pulled to his chin.

And the ache was there again.

Not vague.
Not theoretical.

Absence.

Joseph decided he did care for his family.

He hadn’t known deciding would do this.

He hadn’t realized love was a door you could open and never close again. That once you admitted it—once you let it be true—the missing would become physical.

He saw them like quick strikes behind his eyes.

His mother’s hands in warm water.
His dad’s laugh half-covered by a cough.
A sibling calling his name from another room like it was nothing special.

Normal.
Mundane.

And now unreachable.

The weight bred contempt the longer it sat there.

For this world.
For this body.
For the way the day would ask things of him like nothing had been stolen.

Joseph breathed in through his nose—slow, careful—like if he breathed wrong, something inside him would split open.

He didn’t cry.

Not yet at least, but it felt it there—waiting.

The yearning stayed in his chest like a bruise the day kept pressing.

The day passed.

Morning chores. Midday tasks. Eli giving him small work that kept his paws busy. Chatter filling silence with talk. Fight passing by like weather. The camp moving with the steady indifference of survival.

Joseph did what he was told.

He cut kindling. He carried bundles. He ate when food was put in front of him.

And the ache stayed.

It sat in his ribs when he lifted wood.
It sat behind his eyes when he looked at the sky too long.
It sat in his stomach when he swallowed bread that tasted like nothing.

The evening sat under everything like a rock on a wound.

Flint Water.

A place to speak openly.

He'd promised Soot that he would spread the gospel in town today—when the light was soft and people were lingering, when voices carried but the street wasn’t at full boil.

Joseph had not wanted to.

Being seen felt like stepping into a trap.

But he’d relented anyway—because he believed he should be doing it. Because he’d told Soot about a God who didn’t hide, and it felt like hypocrisy to keep his faith tucked behind a tent flap.

So the whole day, under every task, under every breath, the evening crawled closer.

As the sun tilted and shadows stretched long, Joseph’s hands started to shake—not from cold, but from time finally reaching him.

He found Eli near the edge of camp, where the trees started to tighten.

Eli looked up before Joseph even spoke.

“What.”

Joseph swallowed. His throat already felt scraped raw just from existing.

“I’m… I’m going into Flint Water,” he said.
“For a bit.”

Eli’s eyes held him for a beat too long.

“Stay out of trouble.”

Joseph nodded once and huffed as he walked away.
He knew what that meant.
He knew that was exactly what he was going to do.

Flint Water in the evening wasn’t quiet so much as it was settling.

Stalls half-shuttered. Lanterns being lit. Footsteps slowing. People speaking in tired, practical tones. The river caught the last light and dulled it to metal.

Joseph stayed to narrower paths, keeping his eyes down, letting groups pass before he crossed.

Soot had chosen a place out of sight: a cut between buildings where walls leaned in, where the air smelled damp and old—river stone, stale grain, wet wood. A lane that ended in stacked crates near the bank, hidden enough to talk before stepping into open air.

Joseph leaned his shoulder against the rough wood and waited.

Before Soot arrived, a voice carried from around the corner—female, sharp with affection and exhaustion at the same time.

“Joker, honey—don’t touch that. You’ll burn yourself.”

It wasn’t his mother.

It wasn’t even meant for him.

But his lungs forgot how to move anyway.

The shape of it—the name held like something loved—hit him so hard his vision blurred instantly, like his eyes had been waiting all day for permission.

His throat tightened. His jaw clenched.

No. Not here. Not now.

A tear slid down his muzzle anyway.

Then another.

His chest hitched—too sharp, too fast. His body tried to swallow the sound and failed. A small, strangled whimper leaked out through his teeth like a dog.

Joseph slapped a paw over his mouth.

Too late.

His shoulders shook again, harder this time, and he fought it like he could physically shove grief back down his throat. He pressed his tongue hard against his palate until it ached. He forced air through his nose.

But his breath stuttered, breaking into uneven little pulls that wouldn’t smooth out no matter how hard he tried.

Another whine, thin and broken, that wouldn't hold.

He hated it.

He pressed his forehead to the crate, as if pressure could pin the tears in place.

The whimpering kept slipping out anyway, stifled and ugly—caught behind his paw, vibrating in his jaw. Every time he thought he’d caught it, another one came, smaller, more helpless.

His chest spasmed. His throat burned.

He tried to swallow and it scraped like swallowing something sharp.

The tears didn’t stop. They ran and ran, warm into his fur, gathering in his jawline, dripping onto his sleeve.

Joseph shook his head once—small, furious, like he could shake it out of himself.

It didn’t work.

A wet, strained gasp tore out, and his paw couldn’t fully smother it.

He squeezed his eyes shut so hard white sparks burst behind his lids.

He forced a deep breath and released it slow.
Again—in. Out slow.
Folding it up, packing it away.

The shaking quelled.

The tears didn’t stop right away.

They kept coming in quiet waves, and every so often a tiny whine still slipped loose like a twitch.

But Joseph didn’t let it turn into sound again.

He wiped his face with his sleeve, angry at the wetness, angry at the proof.

One more inhale.
One more exhale.

A beat where he didn’t move.
A beat where he didn’t think.

Then he straightened, slow.
He drew a breath.
Barely under control.

Footsteps scuffed in the lane.

Joseph went still, swallowing hard.

Soot slipped into the cut between buildings like smoke.

Black fur. Bright eyes. Posture already sharpened with purpose.

She took one look at him and her expression changed—just a fraction.

“You look… rough.”

“I’m fine,” Joseph said too fast, voice thick.

Soot’s gaze narrowed--head tilted.

“Sure you are.”

Joseph stared past her toward the street, pretending the river steps were the only thing that mattered.

Soot stepped closer—present, stable.

“So,” she said, like she was talking about coin or weather.
“You ready?”

Joseph’s stomach turned.
He nodded once. Small.

Soot’s mouth twisted like she could taste his fear.

“Don’t do that,” she said.

Joseph blinked.

“Do what?”

“That little rabbit nod,” she snapped.
“You’re not goin’ out there to apologize for breathin’. You’re goin’ out there to say somethin’ true.”

Joseph’s ears dipped.

“I don’t want to—”

Soot’s eyes flashed.
Then—briefly—something softer moved behind them.

Not pity.
Not patience.

Something like recognition.

She built a wall over it immediately.

“Tough,” she said.
“You said you would.”

Joseph sighed.

“I know. I just…” He swallowed, throat tight.
“I’m not good at talking to crowds.”

Soot tilted her head at him, irritation already sharpening her posture.

“You’re good at talkin’ to me.”

Joseph’s jaw tightened.

“Last I checked,” he said, tired, almost matter-of-fact,
“you were a crowd of fur, not people.”

It wasn’t meant as an insult.
He was just… done.

Soot went still.
Her ears angled back a fraction.

Joseph’s expression shifted, just slightly.
That was sharper than he thought it’d be.

For half a second, something like regret flickered in his eyes.

Then Soot snapped back, voice clean and edged.

“Watch it, fox.”

The flicker vanished.

“Yeah, yeah,” Joseph said dismissive, looking past her toward the main strip.

Soot studied him a moment longer.

Her eyes narrowed—not offended so much as recalibrating.

“That ain’t fear,” she said, quieter now.
“That’s resentment.”

Joseph didn’t answer.
His ears dipped, but he didn’t look at her.

Soot exhaled through her nose, sharp.

“Look,” she said, straightening, tone snapping back into familiar hardness.
“You wanna be angry at the world? Fine. Do it after.”

She jerked her chin toward the street.

“Right now you got a job.”

Joseph’s paws curled slightly at his sides.

Soot stepped closer—not gentle, but focused.

“You think I ain’t scared of them?” she said, voice low and fast.
“You think I like standin’ where every eye’s waitin’ for me to slip?”
“But this ain’t about them likin’ you.”
“It’s about whether you believe what you’re about to say.”

Her eyes locked onto his.

“You do. Or you wouldn’t be hurtin’ like this.”

Joseph swallowed. His throat still felt raw.

Soot took a half step back, reclaiming distance like she’d revealed too much by accident.

“Go,” she said, flat but steady.
“Say it clean. Don’t spit it.”

Joseph hesitated only a second longer.

Then he turned toward the street.

Soot slipped back into the shadows at the edge of the lane, arms folding loosely across her chest.

Her posture looked indifferent.
Her eyes were anything but.

“Don’t make me regret backin’ you,” she muttered, just loud enough for him to hear.

Joseph took a breath, then stepped into the open.

The river steps sat at the edge of a small open space where the street widened just enough for people to pause without blocking everything.

Just open enough that voices carried.

Joseph stood where the flickering lantern light hit his face and immediately felt exposed.

Eyes turned.
Just a few, but it was enough.

A badger on a bench. A raccoon tying a bundle. Two coyotes lingering near a post, talking with that easy confidence people had when the world hadn’t asked anything painful of them today.

Joseph’s mouth went dry.
He forced his paws still and opened his mouth.
Nothing came.
His heartbeat filled his ears until it drowned his thoughts.

Joseph looked around.
He found Soot, distant, pretending not to pay attention.
She turned her head to him, barely, and nodded.

Go on, he could almost hear her say.

Joseph swallowed and forced sound out before fear could lock it.

“There’s a God who—”

His voice cracked.
Heat crawled up his ears.
He tried again.

“There’s a God who sees you,” he pushed out.
“He isn’t bought. He isn’t traded. He isn’t like—like the shrines.”

A badger snorted.

“Sure,” someone muttered.
“And what’re you sellin’?”

“I’m not selling anything,” Joseph said too quickly.
“I’m just—He’s real, and He—”

A voice rang out from the side—loud, sharp, amused.

“Oi! That the little fox what didn’t bow?”

Joseph’s stomach dropped.

One of the coyotes had stepped forward a fraction, tall and rangy with a grin that didn’t feel friendly.

His eyes flicked over Joseph like he was measuring how much fun he could get out of him.

“Thought you’d be gone by now,” the coyote called.
“Or dead.”

A few chuckles rose—uncertain, testing.

Joseph’s throat closed.
He took one step back without meaning to.
The open air suddenly felt like it had teeth.

And panic made him stupid.

He went straight to Soot.
He cut across the edge of the space, beelining to where she stood in shadow.

Soot’s eyes flashed—sharp, alarmed.
She didn’t answer him.
She moved.
Soot turned and walked away around the nearest building like she didn’t know him, like she’d never seen him in her life.

Joseph stopped short, caught mid-step.
His chest tightened.
For one awful moment, his mind supplied the worst answer with perfect ease.

She left.

His ears rang. His paws went cold.

Then—faint, from the darkness of an alley beside him—a hiss.

“Fox.”

Joseph jerked his head.

Soot was half-hidden in the alley mouth, eyes bright in the dark.

Joseph stepped into the alley, heart pounding.

“Not there,” she snapped under her breath.
“Not to me. You wanna talk, you come here.”

Joseph nodded too quickly.

Soot’s eyes narrowed.

“And don’t do that either.”

Joseph swallowed.

“They’re eatin’ you alive,” she said, not unkindly. Just factual.

“I know.”

“You’re lettin’ ’em.”

Joseph’s jaw tightened.
For a second he just stood there, chest rising and falling too fast.
Then it came out—desperate and too honest.

“Maybe you should do it.”

Soot blinked once.

Joseph pushed through before he lost the nerve.

“You have the fire for it,” he said.
“You don’t freeze up. You actually—” He gestured vaguely toward the street.
“You want this.”

Soot stared at him.
Her voice, when it came, was level.
Almost too level.

“You forget who I am?”

Joseph hesitated.

Soot’s ears angled back just slightly—not in shame, but in cold recognition.

“They don’t hear a ‘fire,’ fox,” she said.
“They hear ‘angle.’ They hear ‘trick.’”

Her mouth twitched without humor.

“Soon as I open my mouth about God, it won’t matter what I say. It’ll be ‘What’s she sellin’ now?’”

Joseph's head dropped with sigh.
He looked toward the mouth of the alley where Ridge’s voice still drifted in and out of the evening air.

“So it’s me,” he muttered.

Soot followed his gaze.

“You hear what he called you?”

Joseph’s shoulders tightened.

“‘The one who didn’t bow,’” she said.

A beat.

“Lean into it.”

Joseph frowned.

“What?”

Soot turned fully toward him now.

“You ain’t just some fox babblin’ about a new god. You’re that fox.” Her voice went razor-clean.
“The one who stood when priests told you to fold.”

Joseph swallowed. His throat still hurt.

Soot’s eyes locked onto his like she was pinning him in place.

“Make ‘em deal with that first.”

A beat.

“Go back out. And don’t you dare shrink.”

Joseph hesitated—just long enough to feel the terror.

Then he nodded once and stepped out of the alley.

Soot slipped back into motion too—peeling away from the alley mouth, melting to a different shadow at the outskirts, watching from distance.

Joseph walked back into the open.
His paws wanted to turn him around.
His chest wanted to collapse.
But Soot’s words stuck in his ribs like a hook.

Lean into it.

Ridge’s grin widened when Joseph returned.

“There he is,” Ridge called.
“Little shrine-defier.”

Joseph’s heart slammed.
He lifted his chin anyway.
His voice came out louder than it had any right to—thin, shaking at the edges, but carrying.

“I am the one who didn’t bow.”

The chuckles faltered.

A few heads turned more fully now, attention sharpening.

Joseph’s hands trembled at his sides; he curled his claws into his sleeves and kept going.

“I didn’t bow because what you’re bowing to can’t hold you,” he said, voice catching, then steadying.
“It can’t see you. Doesn't love you.”

For a heartbeat—one clean, impossible heartbeat—he was doing it.

People listened.
Not kindly.
But still listening.

Joseph’s chest burned with something that wasn’t just panic.
Something like momentum.

Then Ridge laughed again—short, sharp, dismissive—and the sound cracked the fragile balance.

“Oh, listen to him,” Ridge called.
“Like he’s somebody.”

A different voice chimed in, cutting.

“Yeah—somebody who thinks he’s better than us.”

Another snort.

“Think your god’s gonna save you from teeth and winter?”

The attention sharpened into pressure.
Joseph’s mind started to scatter.

He knew he had an answer, and he tried to give it, but words piled up wrong in his mouth.
His throat tightened again.
He heard himself start to ramble.

He saw eyes glaze.
He saw a badger’s mouth twist like he’d already decided Joseph was an annoyance.

Joseph’s voice faltered.
He backed up—one step, then two—until he was standing at the alley mouth again, breath coming too fast.

He stepped inside.

The shadows swallowed him.

Soot was already there, like she’d been waiting for the moment he cracked.
She met him halfway in the alley, eyes narrowed.

Joseph’s breath shook.

“I did—” he started.
“I tried—”

“You did better,” Soot cut in, quick and sharp. Then, quieter, with something almost grudging under it:
“For a second.”

Joseph swallowed.

“It didn’t last.”

Soot’s jaw clenched.

“It never lasts the first time.”

Joseph stared at her, anger and shame tangling together.

“I can’t keep doing this.”

Soot’s eyes flashed.

“Yes you can.”

Then it started, rising in Joseph's thoughts--bubbling up like magma.

Of course you’d say that. You’re not the one out there.
You get to hide and I get to be torn apart.
You don’t even have to pay for this. I do.

Joseph snapped at himself, vicious.

No! Stop it! Don’t think like!

But the thoughts still bit at him.

Soot watched his face like she could see the war happening behind his eyes.
Then her voice dropped—fast, controlled.

“Fox. You get one sentence. That’s it. One clean sentence. You don’t debate. You don’t answer every dog in the street. You say the truth and you let it land.”

Joseph’s mouth went dry.

Soot leaned closer, and for half a second the hardness slipped and something real showed through.

“I need you to do this,” she said, barely audible.

Then the wall snapped back up.

“Go,” she hissed.
“Before you talk yourself into bein’ a coward.”

Joseph flinched at the word.

Then he turned and stepped out of the alley.

Soot slipped away too—peeling off into the outskirts again, watching from distance, careful to never be seen leaving with him.

Joseph went out again.

One sentence.
He tried to keep it simple.

“There’s a God who came close,” he said, voice shaking.
“Who didn’t stay far away.”

Ridge scoffed.

Someone else cut in.

“So where’s He now?”

Joseph’s thoughts scattered. His mouth opened.

Too many answers.
Too many ways to say it wrong.

A laugh rose from the edge of the space—different from Ridge’s, but joining him.

Joseph’s face heated.
His throat closed.

But he didn’t run back.

He stayed there—because if he ran, he’d prove them right.
Because the alley felt like a leash now.
Because he could feel Soot watching from somewhere wide, and he hated that he needed it.

His mind started to spiral right there in the lantern light.

She’s making you do this.
She’s not the one bleeding.
No—stop it.
You’re doing her job.
She picked you because she’s safe and you’re disposable.

Joseph’s ears rang.

His chest ached—home-ache, grief-ache—and shame layered on top like wet cloth.

He tried to speak again and nothing came out.

He stood there with his mouth half open and no sound, because he was overwhelmed by eyes, by noise, by his own mind turning on him.

And then—like a spark—he remembered something Soot had said earlier, sharp as a whip:

You’re goin’ out there to say somethin’ true.

You said you would.

It hit him wrong now.
Not courage.
Pressure.
And then, he remembered—

Soot walking away from him in the open.
Like she didn’t know him.
The hiss from the alley.

Not there.

The rule.
The distance.
And again—

They don't hear 'fire.' They hear 'angle.'

Joseph’s chest tightened.

If they saw him with her—
If they decided he was hers—

They'd hear trick.

Joseph turned.
Not back toward the river steps.
Toward the shadows where she kept herself apart.
He didn’t even fully understand what he was doing until he was doing it.

Soot’s eyes widened.
Joseph lifted his voice—just enough to carry.

“You know what?” he said, turning so the river steps could hear.
“You want to laugh? Fine.”

Soot’s head snapped toward him.
And in her face—
Panic.
Real panic.
Real fear.

Soot made a choice in a heartbeat.
Her voice cut through the air, loud and ugly on purpose.

“Get away from me, you creep!”

The words hit Joseph like a thrown stone, and they hurt… or shouldn't they have?
Joseph felt them land, but not like pain.
He couldn't understand it, but it felt more… invigorating.
It felt freeing.

It felt like power.

Joseph blinked, startled.

Then he laughed.
A real laugh—short, sharp, unhinged at the edges.

“What’s wrong?” he called, voice light, stepping closer.
“Afraid of lil’ ol’ me?”

Soot’s eyes flashed—furious and frightened all at once.

“Get away!” she shouted, louder now.
“Get away from me!”

She ran.

Joseph chased.
Because for one terrible moment, he felt free.

Free of being pushed.
Free of being watched the

“right” way.
Free of having to be good.

“Soot!” he called, breathless, laughing again.
“Come on—”

A hand caught his scruff.

Joseph’s whole body jerked.

A sharp, involuntary yip—shot out of his muzzle as his legs flew out from under him.

He slammed onto his back, breath punched out of him, spine jolting against hard ground.
A paw, heavy on his chest, pressed him into the dirt.

Ridge loomed over him.
No grin now.
His eyes were hard, focused—protective in the worst way.

“You stay away from her,” Ridge growled, low enough that it wasn’t for the crowd anymore.
“You hear me? You don’t chase her.”

Joseph’s paws scrabbled uselessly at the dirt, panic cold in his veins.

Behind Ridge, Soot had stopped.

She turned back, eyes blazing.

“Ridge!” she shouted.
“Let him go!”

Ridge didn’t look away from Joseph.

“He was chasin’ you.”

“I don’t care,” Soot snapped. Her voice cracked sharp, and for half a second the mask slipped—raw fear under fury.
“Let. Him. Go.”

Ridge’s jaw tightened.

He hesitated—because Soot’s voice hit something in him that forced him to pause.

His grip loosened just enough.

Joseph didn’t wait for more.

He twisted, shoved his body sideways, wriggled out from under Ridge’s weight like prey slipping a jaw.
He hit all fours and bolted down the streets of Flint Water.

Gone.

Soot stood rigid.

Ridge straightened, chest heaving like he’d just won a fight he didn’t fully understand.

Soot stared into the darkness Joseph had vanished into.

For a beat, she didn’t move.

Then panic—held back by anger—flooded in.

Her chest felt too small.
Her throat tightened.

No.
No, no, no!
Not again!

Soot turned on Ridge like he was the only solid thing left to blame.

“What did you do?” she snapped, voice shaking with fury she couldn’t keep clean.
“What did you say to him?”

Ridge bristled immediately.

“I told him to leave you alone.”

“You slammed him into the ground!” Soot hissed.
“He’s half your size, Ridge!”

“He was chasin’ you,” Ridge shot back, defensive now, fear turning into anger.
“What was I supposed to do—just watch?”

Soot’s eyes burned.

“You don’t get to decide what I need,” she said, voice low and poisonous.
“Not like that. Not with me.”

Ridge’s jaw tightened.

“Then what do you want?” he snapped.

Soot’s mouth opened—

And nothing came out.

Because what she wanted was impossible to say in front of the river steps and the lantern light.

Her gaze flicked once toward the darkness where Joseph had gone.
Her stomach twisted.
Inside—where no one could see—the blame turned inward like a knife.

I pushed him.
I knew he was already bleeding.

And the fear underneath was worse than the crowd, worse than Ridge, worse than her reputation.

Because it wasn’t just Joseph she might’ve lost.

It was the only place she’d started to believe she could be seen and not destroyed.

Soot forced her face back into hardness, because softness would ruin her.

“Get out of my sight,” she said, low and deadly.
“Before I forget you ever mattered.”

Ridge’s posture stiffened—pride flaring.

Then he turned and walked away, making sure he looked like he’d chosen to leave.

Soot stood alone as lanterns flickered and the river kept moving.

And in the space where he’d stood, something in her burned again.

entry.content:
The Long Walk

The morning opened wide around them—an autumn field under a bright, cold sun.
The air carried a crisp, metallic bite that slipped clean through fur and cloth.
Grass bowed in the wind, dull golds and browns rolling in slow waves beneath a ridge of trees holding the last of their faded rusts and dry greens.
A few stood bare already, branches thin and skeletal.
Cedar drifted faintly on each passing breeze.

Wooden wheels clattered along the dirt path.
Eli hauled the lead cart by its long handles, leaning half his weight into each step.
The red wolf’s broad shoulders and long, steady gait made the effort look easy.
Fight followed with the second, paws braced on the grips, tail flicking at every rock that rattled the load.

Joseph came last with Snout and Chatter—not that he was deliberately falling behind.
His legs simply refused to behave.
Even after a night of “practice,” every step on fox paws felt like learning to walk all over again.
Balance wobbled.
Toes weren’t where he expected them to be.
And the ground always seemed to tilt unexpectedly.

He leaned heavily on the walking stick he found on the way.
The clothes they’d given him—simple trousers tied at the ankle and a loose tunic—helped him feel less exposed, but the autumn wind still cut through them. So he still kept the blanket wrapped around his shoulders, held tight like a shield.

Chatter had no such slow pace.
The otter skittered from one side of the path to the other, talking almost faster than he breathed.

Questions

“So when you said you didn’t have fur—none?”
“Not even on your arms? Or tail—wait, you didn’t have a tail either, right?”
“Didn’t that feel weird?”
“Also, did bein’ outside feel cold all the time?”
“Like, did you feel naked not havin’ any fur? And how’d you—”

Joseph opened his mouth to answer one of those questions—he wasn’t sure which—but Chatter had already launched into the next.

“—and is bein’ tall better? Or is bein’ small better?”
“Oh! What’s it like havin’—y’know—flat ears?”
“Do they even move?”

Joseph blinked, processing maybe half of that.

“Uh—well—sorta—”

Chatter leaned closer, eyes glowing with fascination, steps bouncing like he had springs in his ankles.

Snout cut in with a sharp, “Chatter. Ease up.”

Chatter skidded to a halt, ears folding.

“Oh. …Right.”

Then he darted ahead to trail behind Fight instead.

The quiet that followed wrapped Joseph like much-needed warmth.

Snout slowed her steps to match his.
The coyote’s lean frame moved with an easy, rangy stride, her ears swiveling at every sound in the treeline.

“You keepin’ up?” she asked.

Joseph nodded, though he wasn’t sure it was true.
Snout kept pace beside him, her eyes still scanning the treeline now and again.

It made him realize he had no idea where they were even headed.

“Where… are we going, anyway?”

Snout glanced down the road.

“Flint Water. Small city couple hours ahead. It’s where we’re based.”

“Like… home?”

She shrugged one shoulder.

“Closest thing to it. We do most o’ our work outta there.”

Joseph considered that, tapping the stick lightly against the ground as he walked.

“What kind of work?”

Snout blew out a slow breath, as if choosing her words.

“We’re a sort o’ contracted law-enforcers. Keep the peace. Track down criminals.”
“Sometimes take bounties if they line up with our route.”
“Folks call on us when somethin’ goes wrong.”

Joseph blinked, surprised.

“Like… sheriffs?”

Snout made a so-so motion with her paw.

“Somethin’ like that. Just… less paperwork.”
“We go where the work leads us.”

Kin

They walked a bit more after that, the explanation settling quietly between them.

Only then did Snout speak again.

“You got any kin where you’re from?”

“Yeah. My parents and two siblings. A brother and a sister.”

Snout’s voice softened.

“You close with ’em?”

A small smile tugged at him.

“Yeah. I… I love my family.”

Snout hummed, thoughtful.

“Then you must miss ’em somethin’ fierce.”

Joseph opened his mouth—then hesitated.

He pictured their faces — his mother's smile, his dad's steady voice—but nothing.

He searched for the feeling he was supposed to have—an ache, a longing, some sharp tug in the chest.
But all he found was a distant fog.
A sense he should miss them.
Nothing more.

Guilt crawled up his throat.

What kind of person doesn’t miss his family?
Do I even care about them?
What’s wrong with me?

His next step caught the edge of a rut. His shaky legs tangled, and before he could correct himself, the world tilted sideways.

He squeaked and hit the ground with a soft oof—startled, but not hurt.

Snout was at his side in a heartbeat.

“Easy. You alright?”

Joseph pushed himself upright, leaning hard on the stick.
His ears burned, more embarrassed by the sound he made than the fall.
His legs trembled once, then settled.

Confession

“I’m okay,” he said quietly—more reflex than truth.

Snout hovered a second longer, making sure he wasn’t about to topple again, then stepped back to give him space.

They resumed walking, and for a moment Joseph considered dropping the conversation, but the weight in his chest didn’t lift.

Finally, he exhaled.

“I do love them my family. I know I do. But…”
He swallowed, searching for the shape of a feeling that wasn’t there.
“I don't know… I just don't miss them as much as… as much as I'd expect to.”

Snout’s ears twitched back—not unkindly, just uncertain.

“Well,” she said after a moment,
“shock can make folk feel strange.”
Her tone was careful, as if she were afraid of stepping wrong.
“Confusion. Numbness. Forgettin’ things you oughta remember. Happens sometimes.”

Joseph nodded, but her words didn’t reach the place in him that needed reaching.

Snout glanced at him again, brow furrowed like she wished she had something better to offer.

“You’ll… sort it out. I reckon.”

It wasn’t comforting. Not even close.

But it was the best she had, and somehow that made it gentler.

Joseph tightened his grip on the stick, eyes low.

“I hope so,” he said.

Fading Light

The hours slipped by in a slow, uneven rhythm—quiet footfalls, the steady creak of carts, the whisper of wind through brittle fall grass.

“Should’ve hit Flint Water before sundown,”
The bobcat's low growl sat just beneath the words.
“If we weren’t slowin’ for him, we’d be there already.”

Snout shot Fight a warning look, and his ears tilted back—not in apology, but in reluctant quiet.

Joseph’s ears dipped.
He tried to lengthen his stride, to match the others—but the moment he pushed himself, his legs wobbled and he fell right back into the same weary pace.

The forest thinned as they walked, trees stretching sparse and bare like fingers clawing at a pale afternoon sky.
The world around them seemed drained of color, washed in soft browns and greys, as if even nature were tired.

Chatter talked now and then, small stories about nothing, but he always trailed off when Joseph didn’t answer.
Snout stayed close, glancing at Joseph every so often to check that he still walked steady.
Eli led the way with a quiet, purposeful stride, Fight trailing behind like a shadow of impatience.

Joseph felt the day gathering in his muscles—small aches along his back and sides, a stiffness he hadn’t expected.
What puzzled him most was how easily the others managed it, their strides steady while his own grew heavier with each mile.
He found himself leaning on it more and more—not for balance, but just to keep upright.

By the time they crested a gentle rise and reached a flattened stretch of road, twilight had already slipped into full night.
The sky opened above them—broad, quiet, studded with a thousand fragile stars.

They kept moving even after darkness fully settled, their shapes drifting lanternless along the path.
Only the stars and a thin crescent moon lit their way, washing the road in pale silver and sharpening the bite of the cold.
Their breaths rose in soft clouds as they walked, steps slower now, quieter—less from caution than fatigue.

After another long while, the land began to change.
Faint fence posts appeared along the roadside—old, leaning, some half-buried in grass.
Then the darker smudges of distant rooftops gathered on the horizon, scattered like a quiet promise: the far-most outskirts of Flint Water.

Still they pressed on a little farther, closing the distance until the silhouettes of barns and watch-lamps were near enough to make out their shapes, though not their details.
Close enough to walk to in the morning.
Close enough to work from.
But far enough to remain unseen.

Only then did Eli call a halt, lifting one hand for the others to stop. He guided them toward a patch of open ground just off the road where the grass sloped gently and the wind broke against a line of scrub pines.

Final Halt

Without a word, Eli, Snout, and Fight began unloading the carts and setting up camp.
They worked with practiced coordination—shaking out tents, driving stakes, gathering what dry sticks and brittle brush they could find.
Soon, the clearing glowed with the first flicker of a small, tight fire.

Joseph hovered close by while the others unpacked the carts, unsure where to stand, unsure how to be useful.
He stepped forward when Eli hauled out the tent canvas, and again when Snout dragged over the wooden stakes, moving more from obligation than strength.

A faint, uneven tremor kept running through him deep through his middle—his lower back and the muscles along his sides struggling to keep him upright.
The strain climbed into his shoulders from all the bracing. Even lifting his stick felt like effort.

Snout noticed first.

“Hold up, fox. You’re shiverin’ out your bones. Go sit by the fire.”

Joseph opened his mouth to argue—though he had nothing to argue with.
He hadn’t even touched anything yet.

Before he could speak, Eli chimed in without looking up from the ropes he was sorting:

“She’s right. You’re spent. Let your legs quit before the rest of you does.”

There was no bite in it—just blunt practicality.

Joseph hesitated. Relief flickered through him, soft and shameful.
He nodded once and stepped back.

“Yeah, ok.”

Chatter darted in next, bright-eyed and ready to fill the gap Joseph left.

“I can get the stakes! Or the brush—no, the stakes—wait, which one d’you want first?”

Fight shifted aside to make room, tail twitching but not dismissive.

“Just—keep to the right side. And don’t trip me.”

“Right side! Got it!”
Chatter chirped—already scooting to the wrong side before correcting himself mid-step.

Snout huffed, but there was the flicker of a fond smile in it.

Sidelines

Joseph watched them for a moment longer, the scene blurring faintly at the edges.
Guilt tugged at him—sitting while they worked—but so did a strange, heavy relief.
His muscles ached all the way down into the joints, an exhausted hum that spread the moment he stopped moving.

He drifted to the fire and sank to his haunches beside the low ring of stones.
The heat touched only the front of his face, leaving his back cold beneath the blanket.

They didn’t need him.
He wasn’t helping.
But sitting still felt like collapsing, like the moment he stopped moving everything inside him sagged at once.

He lingered there a minute or two, staring at the shifting silhouettes of the others as they raised tents and sorted gear.
Each rope hauled, each stake hammered, each quiet exchange of instructions twisted inside him.
He tried to watch.
Tried to stay part of it.
But the guilt only thickened, hot and painful behind his ribs.

He couldn’t sit here and do nothing while they worked—not watch it happen.

Joseph pushed himself up again, the blanket slipping around his shoulders.

“I… think I’m gonna step away for a bit.”

No one looked up.
Chatter was talking, Fight was adjusting a crossbeam, Snout was checking the tent’s stability, and Eli was still tying rope with practiced efficiency.

Joseph turned on stiff legs and limped toward the darker edge of the clearing until the fire’s glow thinned into nothing more than a warm, wavering smear behind him.

Communion

He walked until the sounds of camp faded, until he could breathe without feeling watched.

He settled onto the cold ground, the chill of it reaching up through the thin fur along his legs.
The breeze cut through the clearing in small biting drifts, and he pulled the blanket close until he was almost swallowed in it.

The world was still.
Bare branches swayed gently overhead.
Grass rustled softly.
The stars seemed sharper out here, unmarred by smoke or camp-talk.

Despite the barren season, the land held a quiet, worn beauty.
Subtle. Honest.

It brought a familiar ache into his chest—a reminder of creation, of the God who breathed life into every withered leaf and every distant star.

He didn’t want to pray. Not out loud. Not like this.

But something in him nudged.
Persistent. Gentle. Familiar.

After a long hesitation, he shifted, trying to bow his head to the dirt. His snout bumped the ground first, ruining the motion.
He huffed, frustrated, and eventually rested his muzzle against the earth instead, eyes closed.

“…God,” he whispered, voice small.
“I know You’re here. I know You are. Just… don’t leave me. Please.”

The words came stilted, awkward, pulled straight from a heart too tired to dress them up.

“I don’t know what’s happening. Or where I’m going. Or why I don’t feel the way I should.”
“But I want You. I want You with me. I want You to have Your way—even if I mess everything else up.”

His throat tightened. His body quivered—though not from the cold.

“Just stay. Don’t let me disappoint You.”

He prayed until the words ran dry—until everything inside him had been poured bare.

And when the words gave out, he gave way to something else that filled the silence.

Soft at first, then fuller.

Not English.
Not any language he knew.

A trembling flow of syllables shaped entirely by surrender.

Joseph stayed there, chin against the dirt, blanket wrapped tight around his shaking shoulders, praying in tongues beneath a sky full of stars.

Stirring

Snout padded through the grass, following the faint trail Joseph had left when he wandered off.
His scent clung low to the ground: tired musk, camp-smoke, and that strange edge she still couldn’t name.

She was coming to fetch him.

But she slowed.

Long before she saw him.

Her ears twitched, then pinned halfway back.
The fur along her spine lifted without permission.
The air felt… wrong. Not dangerous, exactly—just charged, humming, like the moment before lightning strikes.
A faint buzzing crawled across her skin, prickling the tips of her whiskers.
Heat pressed at her chest, coiling tight in her lungs.

She stopped walking.

Her throat tightened—not from pain, but from some nameless instinct she’d never felt before.
It wasn’t the cold, or anything she knew.
Just… a pressure in the open air.
Her instincts recoiled, the same way they did before storms or sickness.

Fear?
No, not quite.
Anger?
Not that either, but it flickered at the edges.
A strange repulsion twisted in her gut, like some part of her recoiled without knowing the reason.

For a heartbeat she thought she was imagining it.

Then she took one more step.

And saw him.

The fox laid low to the ground, blanket wrapped around him, head on the ground as though asleep.
Small. Unremarkable.
Yet the moment she laid eyes on him, the buzzing sharpened—hotter, louder—like sparks crackling just under her skin.

It was coming from him.

Snout blinked, breath stuttering, confusion warring with a sudden instinct to back away.
Nothing about him looked threatening.
Nothing explained the pressure behind her ribs.

She stepped forward anyway.

The grass rustled beneath her paw.

Joseph turned at the sound, his ears perked, eyes soft with the faint glow of someone pulled from deep thought.

“Oh. Hi,” he said simply—
as if nothing at all had just shaken the air around him.

Tense Air

Snout didn’t speak.
Neither did Joseph.

Snout just stood there, staring at him with a look he couldn’t name—ears half-pinned, pupils tight, as if she were trying to figure out what he was.
Joseph shifted under the weight of it.

Is there something on me?
He pulled the blanket tighter, brushing at his fur. Nothing.

Her gaze didn’t move.

He glanced behind him. Is something coming?
Just grass, dim twilight, and the quiet sigh of the wind.

His sight returned to her, and still she stared.

“…Is something wrong?” he finally asked.

Snout flinched—barely, but he caught it. Her answer came too sharp, snapping out like a twig under strain.

“You shouldn’t be out here. It’s getting cold.”

Joseph blinked, unsure why she sounded irritated.

“Oh. Sorry. I just… needed a minute. To think.”

Her shoulders eased by a hair. When she spoke again, her tone was steadier, more practiced.

“Supper’s ready.”

“Alright. Thanks,” Joseph said with a faint smile.
“I’ll be over in a second.”

Snout didn’t linger.
She turned quickly, paws brushing through the grass as she moved back toward camp—too fast to be casual, as if distance itself was a relief, as if the air around him was something she needed to escape.

Return

Joseph remained where he was for a moment longer.

The presence settled over him again—warm, gentle, steady.
Like being wrapped in a blanket that reached deeper than fur or skin.
The earlier tension drained from his shoulders, replaced by a slow, quiet peace.
No buzzing, no heat, no fear. Just stillness.

Just God… near.

“Thank You,” he whispered.
“For staying with me.”

The wind stirred softly through the clearing, as if in answer.

After another breath, Joseph stood, gathered the blanket, and made his way back toward the glow of the campfire.

entry.content:
Morning arrived with the same cold it always did.

The air lingered where it was cool enough to bite, but warm enough that frost hadn't troubled the canvas. Joseph woke to damp air and the distant sound of Chatter's voice already running, even before breakfast.

He lay still for a moment, staring at the pale light filtering through the seams.

He whispered:

"Guide my steps Lord. Lead me in your ways, and may your will be done."

Joseph pushed himself up and shook the stiffness from his limbs.

Inside the tent, with the canvas blocking the wind, he felt fine—almost comfortable.
The fur along his arms and chest trapped warmth efficiently, holding it close like a second skin.

This isn't so bad, he thought.
The fur helps.
I'll be fine.

He crawled out into the grey.

The wind hit him immediately—a cutting gust that slipped straight through his fur like it wasn't there.
He yelped and dipped back inside.

A moment later, he emerged again, blanket wrapped so tightly around his shoulders that only his muzzle and ears showed.

He stared at the camp—at Fight already seated by the fire, at Snout chewing something dry and brown, at the cheerful curl of smoke rising into the cold—and made a decision.

Fight looked up as he shuffled over.

"Mornin', icicle."

Joseph didn't answer.
He just found a spot near the fire and—
Sat.
On his haunches.
Forepaws braced against the ground in front of him, supporting his weight the way he'd done every morning since arriving.

It felt natural.
Stable.
Right.

Fight stared at him.
Snout stopped chewing.
Chatter tilted his head, whiskers twitching.

Joseph looked between them.

"What?"

Fight's tail flicked again—slower this time.

"You plannin' to sit like that all day?"

Joseph blinked.

"Like… what?"

Snout and Fight exchanged a glance—quick, loaded with something Joseph couldn't read.

Snout cleared her throat carefully.

"Joseph," she said, her tone gentle in a way that immediately made him wary, "that's how cubs sit. Little ones. Before they learn better."

Joseph stared at her.

"What?"

She demonstrated—spine straight, hind legs folded beneath her, forepaws resting loose in her lap. No support. No brace.

"Most folks sit upright. On their own."

Joseph looked down at himself.
Forepaws flat.
Shoulders hunched.
Weight balanced on his front like—like a child waiting for a story.

Oh.

Heat crawled up his ears.

"I didn't—I didn't know," he muttered.
"No one told me."

Fight snorted.

"Didn't think we had to. Figured it was instinct."

"My instincts are from a body that didn't have a tail or fur," Joseph said flatly.
"So forgive me if I don't know the proper way to be a fox."

Snout's mouth twitched, but she held back the smile.

"No one's forgiving you for anything. It's just—" She gestured.
"You might want to learn. Before someone sees you in town and assumes things."

Joseph's ears flattened further.

Assume things. Like what?
That I'm helpless? That I'm a child?
That I don't belong here?

He already knew the answer to that last one.

He shifted, trying to copy Snout's posture.
His back complained immediately.
His tail got in the way.
He wobbled, caught himself, wobbled again.

Fight snorted.

"Looks like a newborn fawn tryin' to sit pretty."

"Fight," Snout said flatly.

"I'm just observin'."

Joseph ignored them both and kept adjusting.
After a few attempts, he found something close to the right position—back straight, paws free, tail curled awkwardly to the side.
It felt stiff. Wrong.
Like wearing shoes on the wrong feet.
But he held it.

Chatter beamed.

"You look older already!"

Joseph wasn't sure that was a compliment.

Breakfast was dry bread.

Again.

Joseph turned the piece over in his paws, eyeing it.
Same pale crust.
Same faintly sour smell.
Same texture that scraped the roof of his mouth if he wasn't careful.

He bit into it anyway.

This is what we eat, he told himself. 
This is what there is.

But his mind drifted anyway—to warm kitchens, to fresh bread straight from the oven, to butter melting into toast, to the smell of pancakes on Saturday mornings.

His stomach twisted.

Not with hunger.

With something worse.

I miss food, he realized. 
I miss toast. I miss eggs. I miss coffee.

I miss coffee more than I miss my family.

The thought landed like a stone.

He stopped chewing.

What kind of person does that make me?

He stared at the bread in his paws.
Dry.
Plain.
Utterly ordinary.

And yet.

I don't even know if they're okay.
I don't know if they're looking for me.
I don't know if they're—

"You alright over there?"

Joseph startled.

Chatter was watching him, head tilted, whiskers quirked with concern.
Snout had paused mid-chew, and even Fight's gaze had drifted his way.

Joseph blinked, then looked down at the bread in his paws.

"Yeah," he said quickly.
"Fine. Just—thinking."

He took another bite.

Snout held his gaze a moment longer, then shrugged and went back to her breakfast.

The day stretched long after breakfast.

Fight had tasks—repairing straps, checking cart wheels, sorting through gear with the kind of methodical grumpiness that suggested he'd rather be doing anything else.
Chatter followed him like a particularly enthusiastic shadow, asking questions Fight answered in single syllables.

Joseph lingered nearby, uncertain.

He tried to help.

Fight handed him a coil of rope with a worn spot near the middle.
Joseph held it while the bobcat cut a fresh length from a spool, then swapped places to let him splice the new piece in.
The work was slow, deliberate—knots Joseph didn't know, tension he couldn't gauge—but Fight corrected him without snapping, which felt close to kindness.

When that was done, they moved to the cart wheels.
Fight showed him how to check for loose spokes, how to test the hub for wobble, how to tell if a wheel had gone too long without grease.
Joseph listened, asked a few questions, and tried not to get in the way.

It wasn't much.

But it was something.

And somewhere in the middle of it—between one strap repair and the next—Joseph found himself thinking about God again.

Just… thinking.

You're here, he thought, glancing at the sky through bare branches.
I know You're here.
I just don't know what You want.

The wind stirred.
Nothing else.

He kept working.

The dried meat appeared mid-afternoon.

Joseph was helping Chatter stack kindling when he spotted it—a strip of something dark and leathery, laid out on a flat stone near the fire.
Drying.
Curing.
Waiting.

He froze.

Chatter noticed.

"You okay?"

Joseph pointed.

"What… is that?"

Chatter followed his gaze, then looked back at him like he'd asked why water was wet.

"Dried meat," he said.
"You haven't had any yet?"

Joseph's mind went very, very quiet.

They're eating meat.
Everyone here is an animal.
If everyone here is an animal—

He stared at the strip.
Then at Chatter.
Then at his own paws.
Then back at the meat.

Chatter tilted his head.

"…Joseph?"

Joseph's voice came out strangled.

"Where does the meat come from?"

Chatter blinked.

"What d'you mean?"

"I mean—" Joseph gestured vaguely at everything.
"Everyone's—we're all—and that's—"

Understanding dawned slowly across Chatter's face.
His eyes went wide.
His mouth opened.
Closed.
Opened again.

Then his whole body started shaking.

"You thought—" He choked.
"You thought we were eating—"

"I didn't think anything," Joseph said quickly, ears burning.
"I just—it was a moment—"

Chatter slapped both paws over his mouth, but it was too late—laughter burst through anyway, high and wheezing, doubling him over until his forehead nearly touched the ground.

"It's not—" He gasped.
"We don't—Joseph, we're not—"

Joseph huffed, and threw a stick at him.

It missed entirely.

Chatter didn't notice.
He was too busy crying, tears streaming down his whiskers, making sounds that couldn't possibly be healthy.

"It's not—it's not us—" He wheezed.
"It's game—wild ones—deer, rabbit, squirrel—not fox, Joseph, not fox—"

Joseph buried his face in his paws.

"Yes. I get it."

Chatter kept laughing.
And laughing.
And laughing.

Joseph sat there, ears flat, and waited for the ground to swallow him.

It did not oblige.

The moment passed, eventually.

Chatter recovered, mostly, though every few minutes he'd catch Joseph's eye and dissolve into fresh giggles.
Joseph bore it with as much dignity as he could muster, which was not much.

By afternoon, the teasing faded into comfortable quiet.

Fight worked nearby, grumbling under his breath about strap quality.
Joseph watched him out of the corner of his eye—the way the bobcat moved, efficient and sure.
The way his attention kept flicking toward the treeline.
The way he straightened slightly whenever Eli passed within view.

Chatter sidled closer, voice low.

"They're close, y'know."

Joseph glanced at him.

"Who?"

"Eli and Fight." Chatter nodded toward them.
"Fight's been with him longer than anyone."
"Years. Before Snout. Before me."
"Just the two of 'em, runnin' jobs together."

Joseph watched Fight check a cart wheel, then glance toward Eli again—quick, automatic, like checking a tether.

"They seem…" He searched for the word.
"Tied?"

"Yeah," Chatter said.
"That's it. Tied."

He didn't say anything else.

But Joseph noticed the way Chatter's voice softened when he said it.
Like he was watching something he respected but didn't quite understand.

Eli approached mid-afternoon.
The red wolf crossed the camp and crouched beside them, lowering himself to Joseph's level.

"You're settling," he said.

It wasn't a question.

Joseph shrugged.

"Trying to."

Eli nodded, slow.

"I've been thinking," he said.
"About what comes next."

Joseph's ears flicked.

"What do you mean?"

Eli picked up a piece of kindling, turned it over in his broad paw.

"You can't stay hidden forever," he said.
"And you can't live on camp rations and goodwill."
"You need something to do. Something that's yours."

Joseph looked at the kindling in his own paws.

"A job?"

"Eventually." Eli set the stick down.
"I know someone in Flint Water. Runs a print shop—handbills, notices, that sort of thing."
"He's looking for help. Sorting. Organizing. Nothing heavy."

Joseph blinked.

"You think he'd take me?"

"I think you'd surprise yourself." Eli stood.
"I'll talk to him. See if he's willing to take on someone quiet."

He paused, looking down at Joseph.

"You don't have to decide now. Just… think about it."

He walked away before Joseph could answer.

Joseph sat there for a long moment, kindling forgotten in his paws.

A job.
Work.
A reason to leave camp.

The thought felt strange.
New.
Like wearing clothes that hadn't been worn by someone else first.

He didn't know if he wanted it.

But he didn't know if he wanted to stay hidden forever, either.

Night fell slow and cold.
The fire burned low and steady, casting long shadows across the clearing.
Eli sat with his back against a log, legs stretched out, gaze fixed on the flames.
Fight leaned against a cart nearby, arms crossed, tail occasionally twitching as embers popped.
Snout tended the fire with small adjustments, pushing sticks into the glow.

Chatter sprawled on his stomach, chin propped on his paws, staring into the warmth like it held secrets.

Joseph sat apart, blanket wrapped tight, knees drawn up.
Close enough to feel the heat.
Far enough to feel alone.

For a while, no one spoke.

Then Chatter rolled onto his side, whiskers twitching.

"Hey," he said.
"Joseph."

Joseph looked up.

"You know what I've been thinking about all day?"

A bad feeling settled in Joseph's stomach.

"What?"

Chatter's face split into a grin.

"The meat."

Joseph went very still.

Snout glanced up from the fire.
Fight's ear flicked.
Even Eli's gaze shifted—slow, curious.

Chatter sat up, eyes bright with barely contained glee.

"You should've seen him," he said.
"He just—froze. Pointed at the drying meat like it was a—a ghost. Asked where it came from. And then his face—"
Chatter dissolved into giggles.
"He thought—he actually thought—"

"Chatter." Joseph's voice cut through, sharp and sudden.

The otter stopped.

Everyone looked at Joseph.

Joseph's ears were flat.
His jaw tight.
His paws curled into the edge of his blanket.

"I just wanted to know where the meat came from," he said, too fast, too controlled.
"That's all. There was no—I didn't think anything."

The fire crackled.

Fight's brow slowly rose.

Snout's expression was unreadable.

Eli said nothing at all.

Chatter blinked, caught mid-laugh, uncertain now.

"O-oh," he said.
"I just thought it was funny, is all."

Joseph didn't answer.
He stared at the fire, refusing to meet anyone's eyes.
His pulse hammered.
His ears burned.

Stop looking at me.
Just stop.

The silence stretched.

Then Fight snorted.

"Fox," he said, flat and dry,
"you're a terrible liar."

Joseph's head snapped up.

"I'm not lying—"

"You absolutely thought we were eatin' fox."

"I didn't—"

"You pointed at the meat like it bit you."

"It was a confused point—"

"A confused point." Fight's tail flicked.
"That's a new one."

Snout's mouth twitched.

Joseph saw it.

"You're laughing at me," he said flatly.

"I'm not," Snout said, voice perfectly level.
"I'm just… appreciating the moment."

"That's the same thing."

"It's really not."

Chatter perked up again, hope flickering in his eyes.

"So… can I still tell the story?"

" No."

Eli shifted.

The movement was small, but everyone noticed.
The red wolf's gaze hadn't left Joseph—not accusing, not amused.
Just… watching.

"You really didn't know," Eli said quietly.
"Where the meat comes from."

It wasn't a question.

Joseph hesitated.
Then shook his head.

"No. I didn't."

Eli nodded slowly, as if filing the information away.

"Where you're from," he said.
"What did you eat?"

Joseph blinked at the shift.

"Uh. Plants. Mostly. Grains." He stopped. Swallowed.
"Some meat."

The words sat awkwardly in the air.

Fight waited.
Snout watched.
Even Chatter had gone still, sensing something shifting beneath the surface.

Joseph's ears flattened.

"It's just—" He gestured vaguely, searching.
"Where I'm from, meat comes from… animals. Obviously."
"But you don't… I mean, you don't usually think about it like that."
"It's just there. In a shop. Wrapped up. You don't see where it—"

He stopped again, heat crawling up his neck.
He realized, suddenly, what he was saying.

To animals.
Who were animals.

Who probably had neighbors who were deer.
Friends who were rabbits.

His mouth opened.
Closed.
Opened again.

"I—" He looked away.
"This is weird to talk about. With you."

Silence.

Then Fight grunted.

"Weird how?"

Joseph gestured helplessly at all of them.

"You're—" He waved at Fight's fur.
"And I'm—" At his own.
"And the meat is from—" He gave up.
"I don't know how to say it without sounding like I'm describing something horrible."

Snout's expression softened, just slightly.

"We know where meat comes from, Joseph."

"I know you know," he said quickly.
"That's not—I'm not trying to—" He pressed his paws to his face.
"I'm making this worse."

Chatter tilted his head.

"You're worried we'll think you're awful for eating meat?"

Joseph peeked through his paws.

"…Yes?"

Chatter blinked.

"But… everyone eats meat."

"Not where I'm from!"

Fight's brow furrowed.

"Wait.
Nobody ate meat where you're from?"

"No, we did, it's just—" Joseph dropped his paws.
"The animals we ate weren't… us."
"They were different. They didn't talk. Didn't wear clothes. Didn't have names."
"It was just… food."

He trailed off, realizing how thin that sounded.

Eli spoke for the first time.

"And now?"

Joseph looked at him.

"Now what?"

"Now you're here." Eli's voice was calm. Level.
"With us. And we're not so different from the ones you used to eat."

Joseph's stomach clenched.

"I know," he said quietly.
"I think about it."

The fire crackled.

No one spoke.

Then Snout shrugged one shoulder.

"Don't," she said simply.

Joseph blinked.

"What?"

"Don't think about it." She nudged a log with her paw.
"We're not prey. We're not food. We're just… us."
"Whatever we were before, we're this now. That's all that matters."

Joseph stared at her.
It was simple.
Too simple.
And yet.

Fight snorted.

"Besides," he said,
"if you started lookin' at us like dinner, we'd notice."

Chatter gasped.

"Would you eat us, Joseph?"

" No , Chatter."

"Just checking!"

Snout's tail flicked with amusement.
Even Eli's mouth curved, just slightly.

Joseph pulled his blanket tighter, ears still warm.
But underneath the embarrassment, something loosened.

They're not horrified.
They're just… here.

He didn't know what to do with that.

The conversation drifted after that.
Quiet settled back in, comfortable and worn.
Joseph listened more than he spoke, letting the fire's warmth seep into his bones.

At some point, he looked up.

The stars were coming out one by one—faint at first, then brighter, until the whole dome above them was scattered with light.

He found the Little Dipper first.

Then the Big Dipper.

The same stars.
The same patterns.
The same sky he'd stared at from his backyard a lifetime ago.

He didn't realize he'd gone still until Snout's voice came quietly from beside him.

"You alright?"

Joseph blinked.
Looked down.
Nodded.

"Yeah. Just…" He gestured vaguely upward.
"Stars."

Snout followed his gaze.
Frowned slightly.

"What about them?"

"They're the same." His voice came out smaller than he intended.
"Where I'm from. These stars. The same ones."

Snout didn't respond right away.
She just looked up with him, ears angled back.

Chatter noticed and craned his neck.

"What's the same?"

Joseph hesitated.
Then pointed.

"That one. The Little Dipper. And that one—the Big Dipper. We had names for them. The same names."

Chatter squinted.

"They look like… scoops?"

"Yeah." A faint smile tugged at Joseph's mouth.
"Yeah, exactly."

Fight grunted from his spot against the cart.

"Stars are stars. Don't matter where you're from."

Joseph's smile faded.

Don't matter.

But it did matter.
Didn't it?

He looked back up, searching the familiar patterns.
The same stars.
The same sky.

Everything else had changed.
His body.
His world.
His entire existence.

But not this.

It's still the same, he thought. 
Nothing changed up there.

Everything changed down here.

His family's faces rose in his mind—clear as ever.
His mother's smile.
His father's steady voice.
His brother's laugh.
His sister's habit of leaving cups everywhere.

He waited for the ache.

It didn't come.

Not the way it should.

He felt the shape of it—the place where missing ought to live—but it was hollow.
Distant.
Like remembering pain instead of feeling it.

What's wrong with me?

He stared at the stars.

I want to go home.
I do.
I just… don't know how to feel it.

The fire crackled.

No one spoke.

Then, quietly—so quietly Joseph almost missed it—Eli's voice came from across the flames.

"Same stars."

Joseph looked at him.

Eli's gaze was fixed upward, red fur silvered in the starlight.

"Means something," he said.
"Doesn't it?"

Joseph didn't know how to answer.

Means what? he wanted to ask. 
That I'm still connected? That I'm still me?
That nothing's changed and everything has, all at once?

But the words wouldn't come.

So he just nodded, small and uncertain.

"Yeah," he whispered.
"I think so."

Eli didn't push.
Didn't explain.
He just kept looking up, steady and present, as if the stars themselves were enough.

Joseph watched him for a moment.
Then looked back at the sky.

The Little Dipper.
The Big Dipper.

The same.

He sat with that, letting it settle into his chest alongside everything else—the warmth of the fire, the quiet presence of the group, the vast cold spread of stars above.

Same stars, he thought again.
Same God.

The ache still didn't come.
But something else did—small, fragile, barely there.

A thread.
A tether.

Proof, maybe, that he hadn't been completely cut loose.

He pulled his blanket tighter and kept looking up.
Behind him, the fire crackled on.
No one rushed him. No one filled the silence.
They just stayed—present and unhurried—letting him have the moment, letting him hold it.

It wasn't home.
But it was something.
